title: Fitness as a vital sign
goal: Explain why cardiorespiratory fitness is proposed as a vital sign, use the risk ratio per 1 MET to estimate risk differences, and say what cohort data on fitness cannot show.

steps.title: Fitness as a vital sign
steps.text:
[Cardiorespiratory fitness](g:cardiorespiratory-fitness) (CRF) is how well heart, lungs and muscles supply and use oxygen in hard exercise; [VO2max](g:vo2max) is its lab measure. In 2016 the American Heart Association argued that clinics should record it like a [vital sign](g:vital-sign), next to pulse and blood pressure [[c:ross-vital]].

Its case: low fitness goes with more heart disease, death and some cancers. CRF may predict death better than the usual [risk factors](g:risk-factor): smoking, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes. Adding CRF to those factors also sorts people into risk groups more accurately [[c:ross-predict]]. The statement says "potentially stronger", not proven stronger.

claims.text: The AHA statement argues that adding CRF to risk assessment gives clinicians chances to improve patient care and encourage lifestyle change.

evidence.quote: The underlying premise of this statement is that the addition of CRF for risk classification presents health professionals with unique opportunities to improve patient management and to encourage lifestyle-based strategies designed to reduce cardiovascular risk.

claims.text: CRF is a potentially stronger predictor of death than smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol and type 2 diabetes, and improves risk reclassification.

evidence.quote: A growing body of epidemiological and clinical evidence demonstrates not only that CRF is a potentially stronger predictor of mortality than established risk factors such as smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, but that the addition of CRF to traditional risk factors significantly improves the reclassification of risk for adverse outcomes.

steps.title: Fitness in METs: the 1-MET step
steps.text:
Fitness is often written in [METs](g:met). One MET is about 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ [[c:met-35]], so a VO2max of 35 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ is 10 METs.

Kodama pooled 33 cohorts of healthy adults (102,980 people for the death analysis) [[c:kodama-rr]]. For each 1 MET higher fitness, the [risk ratio](g:risk-ratio) was 0.87 for death from any cause and 0.85 for heart events. One MET matches running 1 km·h⁻¹ faster. People at 7.9 METs or more had much lower rates than those below [[c:kodama-79]].

If every extra MET cuts risk by the same ratio, the ratios multiply: 3 METs gives 0.87³ ≈ 0.66.

claims.text: One MET is the oxygen used sitting at rest, set by convention at 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.

evidence.quote: One metabolic equivalent (MET) is defined as the amount of oxygen consumed while sitting at rest and is equal to 3.5 ml O2 per kg body weight x min.

claims.text: Per 1-MET higher fitness (about 1 km·h⁻¹ faster running speed), the risk ratio for all-cause death was 0.87 and for heart events 0.85.

evidence.quote: Pooled RRs of all-cause mortality and CHD/CVD events per 1-MET higher level of MAC (corresponding to 1-km/h higher running/jogging speed) were 0.87 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.84-0.90) and 0.85 (95% CI, 0.82-0.88), respectively.

claims.text: Participants at 7.9 METs or more had substantially lower rates of death and heart events than those below.

evidence.quote: Participants with a MAC of 7.9 METs or more had substantially lower rates of all-cause mortality and CHD/CVD events compared with those with a MAC of less 7.9 METs.

steps.title: From VO2max to risk ratio
steps.problem: A cyclist's VO2max rises from 31.5 to 42 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. How many METs is that gain, and what risk ratio does 0.87 per MET imply?
steps: Risk ratio: 0.87 × 0.87 × 0.87 = 0.7569 × 0.87 = 0.6585, about 0.66, a 34% lower rate of death.
Caution: this compares different people in cohorts, and assumes the same ratio at every MET. It does not promise what training will do to one person.

steps.title: A big clinic cohort: no ceiling
steps.text:
Mandsager followed 122,007 adults sent for a [treadmill test](g:treadmill-test) at one US medical centre between 1991 and 2014 (median follow-up 8.4 years) [[c:mand-design]]. Fitness, estimated from the test, was ranked for age and sex from low to elite. Death risk fell step by step, and elite performers had the lowest risk: HR 0.20 against the low group [[c:mand-elite]]. The authors saw no upper limit of benefit [[c:mand-ceiling]].

But the patients were referred for testing, so they were not a random sample of healthy people. And fitness is not assigned: a [confounder](g:confounder) such as underlying health can raise both fitness and survival.

claims.text: Mandsager's retrospective cohort enrolled patients referred for exercise treadmill testing at one medical centre, 1991–2014, with median follow-up of 8.4 years.

evidence.quote: This retrospective cohort study enrolled patients at a tertiary care academic medical center from January 1, 1991, to December 31, 2014, with a median follow-up of 8.4 years.
Consecutive adult patients referred for symptom-limited exercise treadmill testing

claims.text: All-cause mortality fell as fitness rose and was lowest in elite performers (HR 0.20 against low fitness).

evidence.quote: Risk-adjusted all-cause mortality was inversely proportional to cardiorespiratory fitness and was lowest in elite performers (elite vs low: adjusted hazard ratio [HR], 0.20; 95% CI, 0.16-0.24;

claims.text: The authors report no observed upper limit of benefit from fitness.

evidence.quote: Cardiorespiratory fitness is inversely associated with long-term mortality with no observed upper limit of benefit.

steps.title: Fitness is not the same as activity
steps.text:
Activity is what you do; fitness is what a test measures. Training raises fitness, but fitness also reflects genes, age and health. Two people with the same weekly activity can differ a lot in fitness.

A fitness test has two strengths: it is measured, not recalled, and it adds to the usual risk factors (see the AHA statement above). It has a catch too: a low score can be an early sign of illness, so low fitness may be a marker of risk as much as a cause of it. For a trained cyclist the practical message is to keep the engine you have built.

points: The AHA (2016) argued fitness belongs beside pulse and blood pressure as a vital sign, because it may predict death better than the usual risk factors.
1 MET ≈ 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ and ≈ 1 km·h⁻¹ of running speed. Each MET higher went with a risk ratio of 0.87 for death.
Risk ratios multiply across METs: +3 METs gives about 0.66 if the ratio per MET holds.
Mandsager found no upper limit of benefit, but the sample was patients referred for tests.
Fitness and activity are related, not the same: genes, age and health shape fitness too.

variants.stem: What does it mean to treat cardiorespiratory fitness as a vital sign?

options.text: Clinics record it routinely, as they do blood pressure
options.why: Right: the AHA wants it in routine risk assessment.

options.text: It replaces the blood pressure and cholesterol checks
options.why: The AHA said to add it to the usual factors, not replace them.

options.text: Everyone must reach a fixed VO2max value to count as healthy
options.why: A vital sign is a measure to track, not a pass mark for everyone.

options.text: It proves that low fitness causes disease
options.why: A vital sign flags risk; it does not show cause.

variants.stem: Which set of risk factors did the AHA statement say fitness may predict death better than?

options.text: Age, sex, height and body weight together
options.why: These were not the factors compared in the statement.

options.text: Resting heart rate, sleep length and daily step count
options.why: These were not named in the statement.

options.text: Smoking, high blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes
options.why: Right: these are the established risk factors it named.

options.text: Family history, stress and alcohol intake
options.why: Not the factors named: the statement compared fitness with the established clinical risk factors.

variants.stem: A runner's VO2max rises from 38.5 to 45.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. How many METs is the gain? (1 MET = 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹)

options.why: Does not divide by 3.5: that is the gain in mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹.
This is the final VO2max in METs (45.5 ÷ 3.5), not the gain.
Multiplies instead of dividing (7 × 3.5).

variants.stem: A cyclist's VO2max rises from 42 to 56 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. How many METs is the gain?

options.why: Does not divide by 3.5.
This is the final VO2max in METs (56 ÷ 3.5), not the gain.
Multiplies instead of dividing (14 × 3.5).

variants.stem: A triathlete's VO2max rises from 24.5 to 35 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹. How many METs is the gain?

options.why: Does not divide by 3.5.
This is the final VO2max in METs (35 ÷ 3.5), not the gain.
Multiplies instead of dividing (10.5 × 3.5).

variants.stem: Assume a risk ratio of 0.87 for each 1 MET higher fitness, the same at every step. What ratio does a gain of 2 METs imply?

options.why: Right: ratios multiply.
Adds the reductions; ratios multiply, so this overstates the drop.
Counts one step only.
This is the reduction for one MET, not a ratio for two.

variants.stem: With the same 0.87 per MET, what ratio does a gain of 3 METs imply?

options.why: Adds the reductions; this overstates the drop.
Right: three ratios multiplied.
Counts one step only.
Takes 3 × 0.13 as the ratio; that is a sum of drops.

variants.stem: With the same 0.87 per MET, what ratio does a gain of 4 METs imply?

options.why: Adds the reductions; this overstates the drop.
Counts one step only.
Right: four ratios multiplied.
Takes 4 × 0.13 as the ratio; that is a sum of drops.

variants.stem: What does Kodama's risk ratio of 0.87 per 1 MET tell you?

options.text: Gaining 1 MET adds 13% to your life span
options.why: A risk ratio compares rates between people, not years of life.

options.text: People 1 MET fitter had a 13% lower rate of death from any cause
Each MET cuts your own risk by 87%
options.why: 0.87 is the ratio that remains, and it compares groups.
It is a relative rate, not a share of people who die.

variants.stem: In Kodama's meta-analysis, a 1-MET higher fitness matched running about how much faster?

options.why: Right: 1 MET corresponds to 1 km·h⁻¹ faster running or jogging speed.
Ten times too small.
This mixes up the 3.5 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ value of 1 MET.
This is a typical running speed, not the step per MET.

variants.stem: What most limits using Mandsager's cohort to tell a healthy rider how much fitness to chase?

options.text: Patients were referred for testing, so they are not a healthy sample
options.why: Right: referral selects patients with symptoms or risk.

options.text: The sample of 122,007 is too large to be trusted at all
options.why: A large sample reduces random error; it does not harm validity.

options.text: Deaths cannot be counted over 8.4 years
options.why: Follow-up of this length is normal for mortality cohorts.

options.text: Fitness was graded, which hides all the differences between people
options.why: Grading by age and sex is standard and kept the gradient visible.

variants.stem: What did Mandsager report about the highest fitness group?

options.text: Its death rate rose again, giving a U-shape
options.why: The authors saw no rise at the top.

options.text: Its death rate matched the high group
options.why: The elite group was lowest of all.

options.text: It had the lowest death rate, and no upper limit of benefit was seen
options.why: Right: elite performers did best, HR 0.20 against low.

options.text: The data could not rank it
options.why: The elite group was ranked and had the lowest risk.

variants.stem: Two colleagues ride the same 4 h a week, but one has a VO2max of 12 METs and the other 9. What best explains the gap?

options.text: Fitness also depends on genes, age and health, not only on activity
options.why: Right: activity is one input to fitness.

options.text: One of them must be misreporting rides
options.why: Same activity can differ in fitness; no misreport is needed.

options.text: Fitness depends only on weekly hours, so one test was wrong
options.why: Fitness depends on more than hours; the test can be right.

options.text: The fitter one rides at a lower MET value
options.why: This would lower fitness if anything; it is not an explanation for it.
